Shape the proposal.

A common course needs many kinds of expertise.

MIND(s) is an invitation to develop a teachable, interdisciplinary First-Year Studies theme. Colleagues can contribute a work, improve a research annotation, test a short unit, or help assess the proposed sequence.

Suggest a source or revision

Submissions use public GitHub issues and require a GitHub account. Include a source link, a short rationale, and the proposed change. Please keep private correspondence and student information out of public submissions.

Contributions that will move this forward

Recommend a teachable work

Identify a specific text, artwork, recording or study. Give a manageable selection, an access route and a clear account of its contribution to the common course.

Test a connection

Develop a short comparison across two methods: musical timing and skilled movement, poetry and perception, cellular coordination and collective behavior, or cultivation and attention.

Strengthen the evidence

Add an important counterargument, a replication, a newer review or a clearer explanation of a study’s limits. Correct a record without treating disagreement as an error.

Connections already available at Lawrence

Matty Wegehaupt’s translation of Hyecho’s pilgrimage account provides a direct scholarly contribution to this proposal. The University of Michigan’s Hyecho’s Journey project credits the 2012 translation volume for its journal quotations. A companion selection could examine observation, religious practice, translation and the limits of interpreting another person’s experience. Read the learning-bank entry.

The 2023 Catholic and Buddhist pilgrimage convocation by Madera Allan and Constance Kassor offers a potential contribution through practice, movement, place and transformation. A MIND(s) unit could develop those connections while preserving the traditions’ histories and meanings.

Lawrence’s archive also includes Madera Allan’s First-Year Studies lecture on Borges. Literary treatments of memory and identity could strengthen a later syllabus revision.

These are possible curricular connections drawn from public records. No participation or endorsement by the named faculty is implied.

Work in stages

  1. Develop the case. Refine this syllabus and source bank with colleagues.
  2. Test a short unit. Gather evidence about reading load, accessibility and cross-disciplinary teaching.
  3. Confirm the process. Establish the actual theme-selection schedule, criteria and governance.
  4. Prepare the proposal. Submit a shared curriculum with works, access plans and teaching support.

Editorial standards

Keep claims accountable

Every research entry links a source and records its date, type, review depth and check date. Empirical observations, theoretical interpretations, preprints and cultural works retain their distinct roles.

We do not infer consciousness from complexity, successful performance or a model’s self-description alone. We also do not treat uncertainty as proof of absence. Competing accounts belong in the same collection.

Keep the collection useful

Teaching annotations identify a concrete use and a limit. Link to authorized texts and recordings. Preserve author names, translation context and the distinction between publication and endorsement.

This edition is manually curated. Its October 2026 check date is not an automatic updating service. Significant additions should receive a new check date and a revision note.

The first edition is a starting point.

The purpose is to make the proposal specific enough to evaluate, teach from and improve.
